newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KLSE studying share settlement rules.
newsitem.headline: KLSE studying share settlement rules.

text.p: The Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange is conducting a comprehensive review of its operating procedures which could result in shortening the settlement period, KLSE chairman Nik Mohamed Din said.

"We're looking at a review of the settlement period," Nik Din told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday. "Whether it's a shortening of the period or some improvement on what we have now, that is what we are reviewing."
Currently, share-buyers have seven days to settle their payments. One proposal is to shorten it to five days.
The shorter settlement period would bring the KLSE more in line with major bourses and is seen as a way to curb excessive speculation, particularly on the Second Board.
Share values on that small-capitalisation index rose 93 percent last year.

"We're looking at the whole process in view of the fact that all counters are now on the CDS (Central Depository System), except for things like warrants and loan stocks -- all equity listings are on the CDS," Nik Din said.
The CDS is the KLSE's scripless trading and settlement system. It does away with physical clearing of trades, allowing brokers to offer more efficient service, the KLSE has said.
The system also allows listed companies to get daily updates of their shareholders.
Nik said he remained bullish about the KLSE in 1997.
"I'm personally confident in the market. Our market very much depends on what happens in the world. But locally, the economy is stable and so is the political situation."
He said he expected another banner year for initial public offerings (IPOS) after a record 92 new listings on the KLSE in 1996.
The KLSE now boasts 722 listings, including warrants and companies and more than 620 companies.

Daily average trading value on the KLSE was 1.9 billion ringgit ($764.28 million) in 1996. The KLSE aims to achieve market capitalisation of 1.25 trillion ringgit by the year 2000, from about 800 billion ringgit last year.
He said the exchange planned to move in May into its new building, which will be officially opened by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad in August.
Other highlights in 1997 could include the introduction of of an over-the-counter market (OTC) and the first foreign companies to list locally, Nik Din said.
Securities Commission chairman Munir Majid said this month a blueprint for the OTC would be announced on February 18.
The OTC, modelled after the highly successful NASDAQ in New York, would allow much more liberalised listing rules and would be primarily aimed at promoting capital-intensive firms.
Unlike the order-driven KLSE, the OTC would be quote-driven, with two-way quotes offered by market makers, analysts said.

"The Securities Commission has had several meetings. I know they're working on it," Nik Din said, adding he did not know if it would be ready for operation by the end of this year as announced earlier.
The KLSE chairman said the Securities Commission was also working out guidelines on the listing of foreign companies on the local bourse.
The government announced last year it would allow such listings, initially with Malaysian-owned foreign entities.
Asked if any foreign firms had expressed interest, Nik Din said: "There have been inquiries but we can't say anything until the Securities Commission comes out with the guidelines."
($1=2.486 ringgit)
